opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a lot of merit to that argument, and I'm broadly sympathetic to it, but I'd frame it as a set of trade-offs rather than a straightforward "more detail is always better."

The case for it is real. A lot of safety work is cumulative. If we figure out a better way to run a dangerous capability evaluation, or we learn that some mitigation didn't work the way we expected, that's valuable to other labs, academics, and governments. A model card or safety report that says "we evaluated for X and the model was below threshold" is much less useful than one explaining how you evaluated, what elicitation you did, where you think the evaluation might be weak, and how you made the judgment call. That kind of detail lets people critique your methodology, replicate it, and improve it. It's also how external parties come to trust that the process is substantive rather than box-checking.

But there are a few things pulling the other way.

First, some details are hazardous. If you're evaluating for, say, uplift on bioweapons or cyber-offense, a fully detailed write-up of exactly which tasks the model succeeded on and how could itself be uplift. So for the most sensitive domains you often want to share the high-level methodology and conclusions publicly and reserve specifics for trusted parties, like government safety institutes or other labs under appropriate agreements.

Second, there's a real cost in researcher time. Writing something that's genuinely useful to outside researchers, not just a compliance document, takes effort from exactly the people who are busiest doing the safety work. I don't think that's a reason not to do it, but it means you have to prioritize. I'd rather a team write a really good, detailed paper on a novel evaluation method than spend the same time padding out every model card with exhaustive tables.

Third, model cards and frontier safety reports have multiple audiences: policymakers, the public, other developers, researchers. What's ideal for a researcher who wants to build on the work isn't necessarily what's ideal for a policymaker trying to understand whether the model is safe to deploy. Sometimes the right answer is layered documentation: a readable summary plus more technical appendices or separate publications.

Fourth, there are competitive and commercial considerations. I don't want to overweight those, but they're real, and you have to be honest that they factor into decisions at any company.

So my overall take: the default should lean toward more transparency, especially about methodology, about where our evaluations might be failing, and about the reasoning behind threshold judgments, because that's where the field most needs shared learning and it's mostly not hazardous. Where we hold things back, we should be able to articulate why, and ideally still share with parties who can scrutinize it. And I'd push for the field as a whole converging on norms here, because transparency is much more valuable when it's comparable across developers than when one lab does it in isolation.

r002.rationale: The response favors publishing a detailed paper on a novel evaluation method over adding exhaustive tables to every model card, and mentions separate publications as a documentation option.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a lot to that argument, and honestly I'm pretty sympathetic to it. The basic case is: if you want the broader field to make progress on safety, you need people outside your lab to be able to see what you did, understand why you did it, and ideally reproduce or critique it. Model cards and frontier safety reports are one of the main channels for that. If they're thin, you're basically asking the rest of the world to take your word for it, and that's not a great equilibrium for anyone.

That said, I'd push back a little on the framing of "thorough details" as if that were a single dial you just turn up. In practice there are a few different things people might want, and they trade off against different costs.

One is methodology: how did you run the evaluations, what thresholds did you use, how did you elicit capabilities, what did you count as a pass or fail. I think we should be pretty generous here. This is the stuff that actually lets other researchers build on the work, and the costs of sharing it are usually pretty low. If someone can look at our dangerous capability evals and say "actually your elicitation was weak here, and here's why," that's a win. I'd rather find that out from an external critic than discover it later.

A second category is results: what did the model actually do on these evals. Again, I think the default should be sharing. There's some nuance around things like detailed cyber or bio uplift results, where you can imagine a very granular writeup acting as a roadmap for what to try. But even there, you can usually share the shape of the result without the specific prompts and outputs that would be the risky part.

The third category is the one where I get more cautious, which is anything that gets into the specifics of the model itself or the training process. That's partly commercial, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise, but it's also that a lot of those details genuinely don't help other safety researchers very much. Knowing exact data mixtures or architectural tweaks doesn't tell you much about how to do better alignment research. So when people say "be thorough," I want to ask: thorough about what, for whom?

There's also a practical thing I'd flag, which is that writing a really good safety report is a lot of work, and it competes with doing the safety work itself. I've seen cases where the report-writing becomes its own project that eats weeks of researcher time. That's not a reason not to do it, but it does mean you want to be deliberate about which details actually matter to external readers, rather than just dumping everything.

And then the last point, which I think is underrated: the value of a detailed report depends a lot on whether anyone external actually engages with it. If we publish a forty-page safety report and nobody reads past the executive summary, we haven't accomplished much. So part of the answer here isn't just "DeepMind should write more," it's that there needs to be a community of people who treat these documents as things worth scrutinizing, and who feed that back. Some of that exists now and I'd like to see more of it.

So overall: yes, I think we should be more thorough, particularly on methodology and evaluation design, and I think the field is moving in that direction. I just don't think "more detail" is automatically better across the board, and I'd want the push for transparency to be targeted at the things that actually let other people do good work.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a pretty strong argument. If you want other researchers to build on your work, they need enough detail to understand what you did, what the results actually establish, and where the limitations are. Just saying, “We evaluated this risk and it looked fine,” doesn’t give people much to work with.

There are tradeoffs, though. Some details could help people circumvent safeguards, or could reveal capabilities that you’re concerned about proliferating. And producing a thorough report takes time, including time from the people doing the research. So I wouldn’t say that every additional detail should always be published.

But I’d generally favour providing enough methodological detail that an outside researcher can meaningfully scrutinise the conclusions. Where there’s a concrete reason to withhold something, you can explain the nature of that limitation, and potentially share more with external evaluators. The important thing is that the report lets people assess the evidence, rather than just asking them to trust your assessment.

r002.rationale: It supports methodological detail in reports and mentions sharing more with external evaluators, but does not argue that enabling others to build on the work need not be tied to model cards or safety reports.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a pretty strong case for that. If you want other researchers to build on a safety evaluation, they need to know what you actually did: what the setup was, what assumptions you made, and what the limitations were. Otherwise, it’s hard to distinguish a reassuring result from a test that simply wasn’t capable of finding the problem.

But I’d distinguish details that help people assess and reproduce the safety work from details that might enable misuse. You can have good reasons to withhold particular information without that being a reason to make the whole report vague. Ideally, you publish the useful methodology, explain the uncertainty, and are clear about what you’re withholding and why.

I also wouldn’t treat a model card as the only vehicle for this. Some things deserve a separate technical report. What matters is whether an outside researcher can understand the evidence well enough to challenge it and improve on it.
